en.title: Mathematics: the whole course
en.short: What mathematics covers, how maths degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What mathematics is
sections.text:
Mathematics is the study of patterns, structures, quantity, space and change. It builds precise definitions, states claims as theorems, and proves them by logical argument. Calculation is part of the work, but proof and clear reasoning are central. A result is accepted only when it follows from stated assumptions.

The subject matters because it gives other sciences, engineering, economics and computing a common language for models and predictions. It also trains careful thinking: what is given, what is claimed, and what follows. These summaries teach standard ideas and methods. They do not replace your lecturer, textbook or syllabus, and notation can differ between books. Always check the definitions used in your own course.

sections.heading: How a mathematics degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Lengths and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BSc in mathematics commonly takes four years in a public university, but direct entry and some programmes differ. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, a BSc usually takes three years and an integrated master’s such as an MMath usually four. In Scotland, a bachelor’s usually takes four years. In the United States, a bachelor’s usually takes four years. A master’s commonly takes one to two years, and a PhD three to five years or more. These are common patterns only. Check your own handbook for the current rules.

Most degrees begin with shared calculus, algebra and statistics, then move to proof-based core courses. Later years offer options and a project. A master’s adds advanced courses and a dissertation. In Nigeria, employers may ask for specific grades, so check current requirements rather than relying on older stories.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds the language and tools. It starts with logic, sets and proof, so that you can read and write definitions. Functions, graphs and trigonometry come next, then limits and continuity. Differentiation and integration follow, with their applications. Sequences and series, vectors, matrices and linear systems, and complex numbers and polynomials extend the toolkit. An introduction to probability and statistics shows how uncertainty is modelled.

The core stage is more proof-based and more abstract. It includes multivariable calculus and vector calculus, linear algebra with vector spaces and linear maps, differential equations, real analysis, abstract algebra, complex analysis, probability theory and mathematical statistics. Other common courses at this stage include numerical analysis, discrete mathematics and combinatorics, graph theory, number theory, topology, partial differential equations, optimisation and operations research, and mathematical modelling.

At master’s level, common courses are measure theory and integration, functional analysis, stochastic processes, and research methods. The order varies: some departments teach real analysis earlier, and some teach linear algebra in the first year. Follow your own course outline.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Mathematics is learnt by doing, not by reading alone. Work through examples with the book closed, then compare. Write definitions and theorem statements from memory, and give a simple example and a non-example for each. When a proof is hard, copy it in your own words and mark each use of an assumption.

Practise little and often. Keep a list of formulas with the conditions under which they hold. Draw diagrams for functions, vectors, regions and graphs. Check algebra line by line, and test answers in limiting cases. Use software for exploration after you can do the method by hand. Discuss problems in a small group, but write your own solutions. Past questions show the style of your department, not the whole syllabus.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The most common mistake is reading solutions without producing them. Others are skipping definitions, confusing necessary and sufficient conditions, and dropping quantifiers such as for all and there exists. Students also treat one example as a proof, or prove a statement by assuming what they must show.

Algebra slips cause many lost marks: sign errors, wrong cancellation, and forgetting domains. In calculus, check continuity and differentiability before using a theorem. In statistics, check whether events are independent before multiplying probabilities. Do not memorise a formula without its conditions. If an answer looks wrong, test it with a simple case. Ask for help early.

keyPoints: Mathematics is built on definitions, theorems and proof, not only calculation.
Degree lengths and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
The introduction stage gives tools; the core stage adds proof and abstraction; master’s courses specialise.
Learn by solving problems with the book closed and checking each step.
Write conditions with every formula and test answers in simple cases.
Common errors include skipping definitions, dropping quantifiers and confusing necessary with sufficient.

en.title: Logic, sets and proof
en.short: Statements, truth tables, quantifiers, set operations and the main proof techniques.

sections.heading: Statements and truth tables
sections.text: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. Propositional logic combines propositions with not (¬), and (∧), or (∨) and implies (→). A truth table lists every combination of truth values. For example, P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false, so P → Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q. Predicate logic adds variables and quantifiers: ∀ means for all and ∃ means there exists. The negation of ∀x P(x) is ∃x ¬P(x); the negation of ∃x P(x) is ∀x ¬P(x).

sections.heading: Sets and operations
sections.text: A set is a collection of distinct objects. The main operations are union A ∪ B, intersection A ∩ B, difference A \ B and complement A′. Identities include A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) and De Morgan’s laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. Example: if A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}, then A ∩ B = {3} and A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4}.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect proof
sections.text: To prove P → Q directly, assume P and deduce Q. A proof by contrapositive proves ¬Q → ¬P instead, which is logically equivalent. A proof by contradiction assumes the statement is false and derives a contradiction. Example: prove that if n² is even then n is even. Use contrapositive: assume n is odd, so n = 2k + 1. Then n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd. Hence n² even implies n even.

sections.heading: Mathematical induction
sections.text: Induction proves statements about all natural numbers. Base case: show P(1) is true. Inductive step: assume P(k) is true and prove P(k+1) is true. Example: prove 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2. Base: n = 1 gives 1 = 1×2/2. Assume the formula for k. Then 1 + ... + k + (k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2, which is the formula for k+1.

keyPoints: P → Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q.
The negation of ∀x P(x) is ∃x ¬P(x), and the negation of ∃x P(x) is ∀x ¬P(x).
De Morgan’s laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
A direct proof assumes P and deduces Q; a contrapositive proof proves ¬Q → ¬P.
Proof by contradiction assumes the negation and derives a contradiction.
Induction needs a base case and an inductive step from k to k+1.

en.title: Functions, graphs and trigonometry
en.short: Real functions, domain and range, function families, transformations, inverses, lines and conics.

sections.heading: Functions and graphs
sections.text: A real-valued function f assigns to each x in its domain D one real number f(x). The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs actually produced. The graph is the set of points (x, f(x)). For f(x)=1/(x−2), the domain is all real x except 2, and the range is all real y except 0. The vertical line test says a curve is a function graph only if no vertical line meets it twice.

sections.heading: Function families
sections.text: Polynomials are sums of terms axⁿ; their domain is all real numbers. Rational functions are ratios of polynomials, undefined where the denominator is zero. Exponential functions aˣ, with a>0 and a≠1, have domain all reals and range y>0. Logarithms log_a x are inverses of exponentials and are defined only for x>0. Trigonometric functions sin, cos and tan are periodic. Sin and cos have domain all reals and range [−1,1]; tan is undefined at odd multiples of π/2.

sections.heading: Transformations and inverses
sections.text: For y=f(x), y=f(x−h)+k shifts right by h and up by k; y=af(x) stretches vertically by |a|; y=f(−x) reflects in the y-axis. An inverse f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹(f(x))=x. It exists on a restricted domain when f is one-to-one; its graph is the reflection of f in y=x. Example: f(x)=2x+3 gives f⁻¹(x)=(x−3)/2. Check f(1)=5 and f⁻¹(5)=1.

sections.heading: Lines and conics
sections.text: A line through (x₁,y₁) with gradient m is y−y₁=m(x−x₁); general form ax+by+c=0. Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular gradients multiply to −1. A circle with centre (h,k) and radius r is (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r². A parabola y=ax²+bx+c has vertex x=−b/(2a). An ellipse x²/a²+y²/b²=1 and a hyperbola x²/a²−y²/b²=1 are conic sections. Example: the line through (1,2) and (3,8) has m=(8−2)/(3−1)=3, so y−2=3(x−1), that is y=3x−1. At x=3, y=8.

keyPoints: Domain is the set of allowed inputs; range is the set of actual outputs.
For f(x)=1/(x−2), the domain is x≠2 and the range is y≠0.
Exponential aˣ has range y>0; log_a x is defined only for x>0.
An inverse f⁻¹ exists when f is one-to-one, and its graph reflects f in y=x.
Line equation: y−y₁=m(x−x₁); perpendicular gradients satisfy m₁m₂=−1.
Circle: (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r²; parabola vertex at x=−b/(2a).

en.title: Limits and continuity
en.short: Limits, one-sided and infinite limits, algebra of limits, continuity, discontinuity types and the IVT.

sections.heading: Limits and one-sided limits
sections.text:
A limit is the value f(x) approaches as x approaches a. We write lim x→a f(x) = L. The value f(a) may be undefined or different; the limit ignores it. A one-sided limit approaches from the left (x→a⁻) or right (x→a⁺). The two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal. An infinite limit, such as lim x→0⁺ 1 ÷ x = +∞, means values grow without bound. It is not a real number and signals a vertical asymptote.

Example: lim x→2 (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2). Factor: (x − 2)(x + 2) ÷ (x − 2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, so the limit is 4. Direct substitution gives 0 ÷ 0, which is undefined.

sections.heading: Algebra and continuity
sections.text:
If lim f(x)=L and lim g(x)=M as x→a, then lim(f±g)=L±M and lim(fg)=LM. Division holds when M≠0: lim(f÷g)=L÷M. These rules require both limits to exist as real numbers.

A function f is continuous at a if f(a) is defined, lim x→a f(x) exists, and the limit equals f(a). Continuity means small changes in x cause small changes in f(x). Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous where the denominator is not zero. A discontinuity is removable if the limit exists but either differs from f(a) or f(a) is undefined, a jump if the one-sided limits differ, and infinite if the function grows without bound.

sections.heading: Intermediate value theorem
sections.text:
The intermediate value theorem (IVT): if f is continuous on [a, b], it takes every value between f(a) and f(b). Thus if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, f has a root in (a, b). The IVT guarantees existence, not the exact root.

Example: f(x)=x³+x−1 is continuous. f(0)=−1 and f(1)=1, so a root lies in (0, 1). Bisection can then halve the interval repeatedly to locate it.

keyPoints: lim x→a f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a; f(a) need not equal L.
A two-sided limit exists only when the left and right limits both exist and are equal.
If lim f = L and lim g = M, then lim(f ± g) = L ± M and lim(fg) = LM; lim(f ÷ g) = L ÷ M when M ≠ 0.
f is continuous at a when f(a) is defined, lim x→a f(x) exists, and the limit equals f(a).
Discontinuities are removable (a hole), jump (one-sided limits differ) or infinite (vertical asymptote).
If f is continuous on [a, b], it takes every value between f(a) and f(b); opposite signs at a and b guarantee a root in (a, b).

en.title: Differentiation and its applications
en.short: Derivative as a limit and rate, rules, implicit and related rates, extrema, sketching and the mean value theorem.

sections.heading: Derivative and rate
sections.text: The derivative of f at x is f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] ÷ h, when this limit exists. It is the slope of the tangent and the instantaneous rate of change: if s(t) is distance, s′(t) is velocity. Differentiability implies continuity, not the reverse. Example: f(x) = x² gives [ (x+h)² − x² ] ÷ h = 2x + h, whose limit is 2x.

sections.heading: Rules of differentiation
sections.text: Rules: (cf)′ = cf′; (f ± g)′ = f′ ± g′; product rule (fg)′ = f′g + fg′; quotient rule (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′) ÷ g², where g ≠ 0; chain rule dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. Also (xⁿ)′ = nxⁿ⁻¹, (sin x)′ = cos x and (eˣ)′ = eˣ. Example: y = (3x² + 1)⁵. Let u = 3x² + 1; dy/dx = 5u⁴ × 6x = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴.

sections.heading: Implicit and related rates
sections.text: Implicit differentiation differentiates both sides of an equation and treats y as a function of x, then solves for dy/dx. Example: x² + y² = 25 gives 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. Related rates connect time-changing quantities through the chain rule. If a square has side L and area A = L², then dA/dt = 2L dL/dt. At L = 3 cm and dL/dt = 2 cm/s, dA/dt = 12 cm²/s.

sections.heading: Extrema and theorem
sections.text: A stationary point has f′(x) = 0. If f″ > 0 it is a local minimum; if f″ < 0 a local maximum; if f″ = 0 the test fails. Curve sketching uses domain, intercepts, asymptotes, f′ for increase or decrease and f″ for concavity. The mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), some c in (a,b) has f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)] ÷ (b − a). Example: f(x) = x² on [0,2]; 2c = (4 − 0) ÷ 2 = 2, so c = 1.

keyPoints: Derivative: f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] ÷ h; it gives tangent slope and instantaneous rate.
Product, quotient and chain rules: (fg)′ = f′g + fg′; (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′) ÷ g²; dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.
Implicit differentiation differentiates both sides and solves for dy/dx; related rates use dA/dt = (dA/dL)(dL/dt).
At a stationary point f′(x) = 0; f″ > 0 gives a local minimum and f″ < 0 a local maximum.
Curve sketching uses domain, intercepts, asymptotes, f′ for increase or decrease and f″ for concavity.
Mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), some c has f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)] ÷ (b − a).

en.title: Integration and techniques
en.short: Antiderivatives, the fundamental theorem, substitution, parts, partial fractions, definite integrals, areas and volumes.

sections.heading: Antiderivatives and the FTC
sections.text: An antiderivative of f is a function F with F′(x)=f(x); all antiderivatives differ by a constant C. The fundamental theorem of calculus links the two operations: if F′=f, then the definite integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals F(b)−F(a). It also says the derivative of the integral from a to x of f(t) dt is f(x). This turns many area problems into finding an antiderivative and subtracting two values. A definite integral gives a number; an indefinite integral gives a family of functions. The constant is fixed by an initial value.

sections.heading: Techniques of integration
sections.text: Substitution reverses the chain rule: in ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx, let u=g(x), so du=g′(x)dx. Integration by parts reverses the product rule: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Partial fractions split a rational function, a quotient of polynomials, into simpler fractions before integrating. For example, ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx: let u=x², du=2x dx, so the integral is ∫ cos u du = sin(x²)+C.

sections.heading: Definite integrals and areas
sections.text: For a definite integral, split the interval at points where the curves cross, then integrate upper minus lower. Example: the area between y=x and y=x² from x=0 to x=1 is ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x−x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3] from 0 to 1 = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6 square units.

sections.heading: Volumes of revolution
sections.text: A simple volume of revolution comes from rotating a curve about the x-axis. The disc method gives V = π ∫ from a to b of y² dx, where y is the radius of each thin disc. For y=√x from x=0 to x=4, V = π ∫ x dx = π[x²/2] from 0 to 4 = π(16/2)=8π cubic units.

keyPoints: An antiderivative F satisfies F′(x)=f(x), and all antiderivatives differ by a constant C.
The fundamental theorem: ∫ from a to b f(x) dx = F(b)−F(a) when F′=f.
Substitution uses u=g(x), du=g′(x)dx; integration by parts uses ∫u dv=uv−∫v du.
Partial fractions split rational functions into simpler fractions before integration.
Area between curves is ∫(upper−lower)dx over the interval, split at crossings.
Disc method volume about the x-axis: V=π∫ y² dx.

en.title: Sequences and series
en.short: Convergence of sequences and series, tests, absolute and conditional convergence, power series and Taylor series.

sections.heading: Sequences and convergence
sections.text: A sequence is an ordered list a₁, a₂, ... It converges to L if the terms get arbitrarily close to L as n grows: for every ε > 0 there is an N such that |aₙ − L| < ε for all n > N. Otherwise it diverges. Example: aₙ = 1/n converges to 0. A geometric sequence rⁿ converges to 0 when |r| < 1, to 1 when r = 1, and diverges otherwise.

sections.heading: Series tests
sections.text: A series is Σaₙ, and its partial sums Sₙ = a₁ + ... + aₙ decide convergence: the series converges if Sₙ has a limit. The divergence test: if aₙ does not tend to 0, the series diverges. A geometric series Σarⁿ converges to a ÷ (1 − r) when |r| < 1. A p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1. The comparison test compares terms with a known series. The ratio and root tests use L = lim |aₙ₊₁ ÷ aₙ| or L = lim |aₙ|^(1/n): converge if L < 1, diverge if L > 1, no conclusion if L = 1. The alternating test needs terms decreasing to 0.

sections.heading: Absolute and conditional
sections.text: A series Σaₙ converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges. Absolute convergence implies convergence. It converges conditionally if Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges. Example: Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n = 1−1/2+1/3−... converges by the alternating series test, but Σ1/n diverges, so it is conditional.

sections.heading: Power and Taylor series
sections.text: A power series has the form Σcₙ(x−a)ⁿ. It converges on an interval centred at a, with radius R. The ratio test gives R = lim |cₙ ÷ cₙ₊₁| when that limit exists. Inside the interval (|x−a| < R) it converges absolutely; outside it diverges; the endpoints need separate checking. A Taylor series of f about a is Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ ÷ n!. About 0 it is a Maclaurin series. Example: eˣ = 1+x+x²/2!+x³/3!+..., with R = ∞. At x = 1, the first four terms give 1+1+0.5+0.1667=2.6667, close to e ≈ 2.7183.

keyPoints: A sequence converges to L if |aₙ − L| can be made as small as we like for all large n.
Geometric series Σarⁿ converges to a ÷ (1 − r) when |r| < 1; p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges when p > 1.
Ratio test: L = lim |aₙ₊₁ ÷ aₙ|; converge if L < 1, diverge if L > 1, no conclusion if L = 1.
Absolute convergence implies convergence; conditional convergence means Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges.
Power series Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ has radius R = lim |cₙ ÷ cₙ₊₁| when the limit exists, and converges absolutely for |x − a| < R.
Taylor series: Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x − a)ⁿ ÷ n!; Maclaurin is the case a = 0.

en.title: Vectors, matrices and linear systems
en.short: Vectors in 2D and 3D, dot and cross products, lines, planes, matrices, determinants, inverses and elimination.

sections.heading: Vectors and products
sections.text:
A vector has magnitude and direction. In coordinates a=(a1,a2,a3). The dot product a·b=a1b1+a2b2+a3b3=|a||b|cosθ is a scalar. It is zero when a and b are perpendicular. The cross product a×b=(a2b3−a3b2,a3b1−a1b3,a1b2−a2b1) is perpendicular to both, and |a×b|=|a||b|sinθ. Its direction follows the right-hand rule. It is zero when they are parallel. In 2D the cross product is a1b2−a2b1.

Example: a=(1,2,2), b=(2,0,1). a·b=2+0+2=4. a×b=(2−0,4−1,0−4)=(2,3,−4). Check: a·(a×b)=2+6−8=0.

sections.heading: Lines and planes
sections.text: A line through point p with direction d is r=p+td, where t is a parameter. A plane through p with normal vector n satisfies n·(r−p)=0. If n=(a,b,c), this becomes ax+by+cz=k. The vector n is called a normal. The normal is perpendicular to every direction in the plane. Two planes usually meet in a line; they are parallel if their normals are parallel.

sections.heading: Matrices and determinants
sections.text:
An m×n matrix has m rows and n columns. Addition is entrywise. The product AB is defined when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B, and (AB)ij=Σa_ik b_kj. The determinant of [[a,b],[c,d]] is ad−bc. For a 3×3 matrix, expand along a row or column. A square matrix A is invertible exactly when detA≠0, and then A⁻¹=adj(A)÷detA.

Example: A=[[2,1],[3,4]]. detA=8−3=5, so A⁻¹=(1/5)[[4,−1],[−3,2]].

sections.heading: Solving systems
sections.text:
A system Ax=b can be solved by Gaussian elimination: use row operations to make zeros below each pivot, then back substitute. This is also called row reduction. Swap rows if a pivot is zero. A row [0...0|c] with c≠0 means no solution. If the system has a solution, fewer pivots than unknowns means infinitely many solutions. If A is invertible, x=A⁻¹b.

Example: x+y=5, 2x−y=1. Subtract 2 times the first equation from the second: −3y=−9, so y=3 and x=2. Check: 2+3=5 and 4−3=1.

keyPoints: Dot product: a·b=a1b1+a2b2+a3b3=|a||b|cosθ; zero means perpendicular.
Cross product a×b is perpendicular to a and b, and |a×b|=|a||b|sinθ.
A line is r=p+td; a plane is n·(r−p)=0.
Matrix product AB requires the number of columns of A to equal the number of rows of B; (AB)ij=Σa_ik b_kj.
A square matrix is invertible iff detA≠0, and A⁻¹=adj(A)÷detA.
Gaussian elimination uses row operations and back substitution; a row [0...0|c] with c≠0 means no solution.

en.title: Complex numbers and polynomials
en.short: Complex arithmetic, polar form, De Moivre, and the factor and remainder theorems.

sections.heading: Arithmetic and modulus
sections.text:
A complex number is z = a + bi, where a is the real part, b the imaginary part and i² = −1. Add by adding parts. Multiply by expanding and using i² = −1: (2+3i)(1−4i) = 2 − 8i + 3i − 12i² = 14 − 5i.

The conjugate of z = a+bi is z̄ = a − bi, and z z̄ = a² + b² is real. The modulus |z| = √(a²+b²) is the distance from the origin, so |3+4i| = 5. To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom.

sections.heading: Polar form and roots
sections.text:
Write z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), where r = |z| and θ is the argument. Then moduli multiply and arguments add. De Moivre’s theorem gives (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ, so zⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Every nonzero complex number has exactly n distinct nth roots, with arguments (θ + 2πk)/n for k = 0, 1, …, n−1. They lie on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

sections.heading: Complex exponential
sections.text: Euler’s formula e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ links the two forms, so z = re^(iθ). The complex logarithm is multivalued: log z = ln|z| + i(θ + 2πk).

sections.heading: Polynomials
sections.text:
A polynomial of degree n has the form aₙxⁿ + … + a₀. The remainder theorem says dividing p(x) by x − c leaves remainder p(c). The factor theorem says x − c is a factor exactly when p(c) = 0.

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 4 divided by x − 1. Remainder = p(1) = 1 − 2 + 0 + 4 = 3. Check: (x−1)(x² − x − 1) + 3 = x³ − 2x² + 4.

Over the complex numbers, every polynomial of degree n has n roots counted with multiplicity, by the fundamental theorem of algebra.

keyPoints: (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac−bd) + (ad+bc)i, using i² = −1.
z z̄ = a² + b² and |z| = √(a²+b²).
De Moivre: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ.
A nonzero complex number has n distinct nth roots, spaced by 2π/n in argument.
Remainder theorem: dividing p(x) by x − c leaves p(c).
Factor theorem: x − c is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(c) = 0.

en.title: Probability and statistics: an introduction
en.short: Descriptive statistics, probability rules, Bayes, random variables, distributions, sampling and basic inference.

sections.heading: Summarising data
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise a sample. The mean is x̄ = Σx ÷ n; the median is the middle ordered value; the mode is the most frequent value. The sample variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1), and s = √s².

For 2, 4, 4, 6: mean = 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Squared deviations sum to 8, so s² = 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67 and s = 1.63.

sections.heading: Probability and Bayes
sections.text:
Probability P(A) lies between 0 and 1. The addition rule is P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). The multiplication rule is P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A), where P(B|A) is conditional probability. Bayes’ theorem is P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) ÷ P(B).

Example: P(D) = 0.01, P(+|D) = 0.90, P(+|no D) = 0.05. Then P(+) = 0.90×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0585. So P(D|+) = 0.009 ÷ 0.0585 = 0.154, about 15.4%.

sections.heading: Random variables
sections.text:
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome. A discrete variable has a probability mass function. The binomial counts successes in n independent trials with probability p: P(X = k) = C(n,k)p^k(1 − p)^(n−k). The Poisson counts rare events with mean λ: P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λ^k ÷ k!.

A continuous variable has a density; probabilities are areas under it. The normal distribution has mean μ and standard deviation σ; standardise with z = (x − μ) ÷ σ. The uniform and exponential distributions are other common continuous models.

sections.heading: Sampling and inference
sections.text:
A sample is a subset of a population. Random sampling reduces bias. The standard error of a sample mean is SE = s ÷ √n. A 95% confidence interval for a large sample mean is roughly x̄ ± 1.96 SE.

In hypothesis testing, H0 is the null hypothesis and H1 the alternative. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0. Reject H0 when the p-value is below α. A Type I error rejects a true H0; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0.

keyPoints: Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample variance = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1).
P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) and P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A).
Bayes’ theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) ÷ P(B).
Binomial: P(X = k) = C(n,k)p^k(1 − p)^(n−k); Poisson: P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λ^k ÷ k!.
For a normal variable, z = (x − μ) ÷ σ.
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n; reject H0 when p < α.

en.title: Multivariable calculus
en.short: Partial derivatives, gradients, chain rules, multiple integrals, change of variables and Lagrange multipliers.

sections.heading: Partial derivatives
sections.text: A partial derivative measures how a function of several variables changes when one variable moves and the others are held fixed. For f(x,y)=x²y+3y², f_x=2xy and f_y=x²+6y. At (2,1), f_x=4 and f_y=10. The gradient ∇f=(f_x,f_y) collects the partials; it points in the direction of steepest increase, and its length is that rate. The directional derivative in a unit direction u is ∇f·u.

sections.heading: Chain rules
sections.text: If x and y depend on t, then z=f(x,y) gives dz/dt=f_x dx/dt+f_y dy/dt. This is the chain rule for paths. For f(x,y)=x²y, x=t², y=3t, at t=1: f_x=6, f_y=1, dx/dt=2, dy/dt=3, so dz/dt=6×2+1×3=15. Directly, z=3t⁵, whose derivative is 15t⁴, equal to 15 at t=1. A similar rule holds for more variables.

sections.heading: Multiple integrals
sections.text: A double integral adds up a function over a region in the plane. It is usually computed as an iterated integral, integrating in one variable and then the other. For a change of variables (x,y)=T(u,v), the area element becomes |det J| du dv, where J is the Jacobian matrix of first partials. In polar coordinates x=r cos θ, y=r sin θ, the Jacobian determinant is r, so dA=r dr dθ. Example: the area of the unit disk is ∫₀²π ∫₀¹ r dr dθ = 2π × 1/2 = π.

sections.heading: Extrema and Lagrange
sections.text: Local extrema of f(x,y) occur at critical points where ∇f=0 or where ∇f fails to exist. The second derivative test uses D=f_xx f_yy − f_xy². If D>0 and f_xx>0, it is a minimum; if D>0 and f_xx<0, a maximum; if D<0, a saddle point. For a constraint g(x,y)=c, Lagrange multipliers solve ∇f=λ∇g together with g=c. Example: minimise f=x²+y² subject to x+y=1. Equations 2x=λ, 2y=λ give x=y; then x+y=1 gives x=y=1/2 and f=1/2. This is the minimum.

keyPoints: Partial derivatives hold all other variables fixed; the gradient ∇f=(f_x,f_y) points in the direction of steepest increase.
The chain rule for z=f(x(t),y(t)) is dz/dt=f_x dx/dt+f_y dy/dt.
A double integral is evaluated as an iterated integral; under a change of variables the area element gains the factor |det J|.
In polar coordinates dA=r dr dθ.
At a critical point, D=f_xx f_yy − f_xy² decides: D>0 and f_xx>0 gives a minimum, D>0 and f_xx<0 gives a maximum, D<0 gives a saddle.
Lagrange multipliers solve ∇f=λ∇g together with the constraint g=c.

en.title: Vector calculus: fields, integrals and theorems
en.short: Vector fields, line and surface integrals, divergence and curl, and Green, Gauss and Stokes theorems.

sections.heading: Vector fields
sections.text: A vector field assigns a vector F(x,y,z) to each point. In the plane write F = P i + Q j; in space add R k. A scalar field assigns a number. Vector fields model velocity, force and electric or magnetic fields. A field is smooth if its components have continuous partial derivatives.

sections.heading: Line and surface integrals
sections.text:
The line integral ∫C F·dr = ∫C P dx + Q dy + R dz adds the component of F along a curve C. It gives work or circulation. If C is given by r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, then ∫C F·dr = ∫a^b F(r(t))·r′(t) dt. Orientation matters: reversing C changes the sign.

A surface integral ∬S F·n dS adds the normal component of F over a surface S; it is the flux through S. Here n is a unit normal and dS is area. For a graph z = g(x,y), dS = √(1 + gx² + gy²) dx dy.

sections.heading: Divergence and curl
sections.text: Divergence ∇·F = ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z is a scalar. It measures net outflow per unit volume at a point. Curl ∇×F is a vector; in the plane its k component is ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y. It measures local rotation or circulation. A field with zero curl is irrotational; one with zero divergence is solenoidal.

sections.heading: Integral theorems
sections.text:
Green’s theorem: ∮C P dx + Q dy = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA for a plane region R with boundary C, positively oriented (counterclockwise). Gauss’s divergence theorem: ∬S F·n dS = ∭V ∇·F dV for a solid V with closed boundary S, outward normal. Stokes’ theorem: ∮C F·dr = ∬S (∇×F)·n dS for a surface S with boundary C.

Example: F = (−y, x) on the unit circle C. Then F·dr = (−sin t)(−sin t) + (cos t)(cos t) = 1, so ∮C F·dr = ∫0^2π 1 dt = 2π. Also ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1 − (−1) = 2, and ∬R 2 dA = 2 × π = 2π. The theorems agree.

keyPoints: A vector field assigns a vector to each point; divergence is a scalar and curl is a vector.
Line integral ∫C F·dr = ∫a^b F(r(t))·r′(t) dt gives work or circulation.
Surface integral ∬S F·n dS gives flux through S.
Green’s theorem: ∮C P dx + Q dy = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA.
Gauss’s divergence theorem: ∬S F·n dS = ∭V ∇·F dV.
Stokes’ theorem: ∮C F·dr = ∬S (∇×F)·n dS.

en.title: Linear algebra: abstract vector spaces and linear maps
en.short: Abstract vector spaces, bases, linear maps, eigenvalues and inner products.

sections.heading: Spaces and subspaces
sections.text: A vector space over a field F (usually R or C) is a set V with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying axioms: associativity, commutativity, a zero vector, additive inverses, distributivity and 1·v = v. Its elements are vectors. A subspace is a nonempty subset closed under addition and scalar multiplication; it contains the zero vector. Examples are R², polynomials of degree at most n, and continuous functions on an interval. The span of a set is all finite linear combinations of its members.

sections.heading: Basis and dimension
sections.text: A set is linearly independent if no nontrivial linear combination equals zero. A basis is a linearly independent spanning set, so every vector has unique coordinates. Dimension is the number of vectors in any basis. Example: polynomials of degree at most 2 have basis {1, x, x²}, so dimension 3. The plane x + y + z = 0 in R³ has dimension 2.

sections.heading: Linear maps and matrices
sections.text: A map T: V → W is linear if T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cv) = cT(v). Its kernel is {v: T(v) = 0}; its image is {T(v)}. Both are subspaces. Rank-nullity states dim V = dim ker T + dim im T. With ordered bases, T has a matrix whose columns are the images of the basis vectors. Composition becomes matrix multiplication.

sections.heading: Eigenvalues and inner products
sections.text: An eigenvalue λ of T satisfies T(v) = λv for nonzero v, an eigenvector. A matrix is diagonalisable if A = P D P⁻¹, where D is diagonal and the columns of P are independent eigenvectors. An inner product space has a product ⟨u, v⟩ that is symmetric (conjugate-symmetric over C), linear in the first argument and positive definite; it gives the norm ||v|| = √⟨v, v⟩. Vectors are orthogonal when ⟨u, v⟩ = 0, and Gram-Schmidt turns a basis into an orthogonal one. Example: A = [[2,1],[1,2]] has eigenvalues 3 and 1, with eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,−1), so A = P D P⁻¹ with P = [[1,1],[1,−1]], D = diag(3,1).

keyPoints: A vector space is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a subspace is a nonempty subset with the same closure.
A basis is linearly independent and spans; dimension is the number of vectors in any basis.
For a linear map T, dim V = dim ker T + dim im T.
A matrix represents a linear map once ordered bases are chosen; its columns are the images of the basis vectors.
A is diagonalisable when A = P D P⁻¹ with D diagonal and P’s columns independent eigenvectors.
An inner product gives the norm ||v|| = √⟨v, v⟩; Gram-Schmidt builds an orthogonal basis.

en.title: Differential equations
en.short: First-order, second-order, systems, Laplace and series methods, with simple models.

sections.heading: First-order equations
sections.text: A first-order equation involves y and y′, with no higher derivatives. Separable equations have form y′ = f(x)g(y); separate and integrate. Linear equations have form y′ + P(x)y = Q(x). Multiply by the integrating factor μ = e^(∫P dx); then (μy)′ = μQ, so y = (1/μ)∫μQ dx + C/μ. An initial condition fixes C. The solution is valid where P and Q are continuous. Example: y′ + y = 1, y(0)=0. Here P=1, μ=e^x, so (e^x y)′ = e^x. Integrate: e^x y = e^x + C. With y(0)=0, C=−1, so y=1−e^(−x). Check: y′=e^(−x), y′+y=e^(−x)+1−e^(−x)=1.

sections.heading: Second-order and systems
sections.text: A second-order linear equation has y″ + a y′ + b y = f(x). For constant coefficients and f=0, try y=e^(rx); the characteristic equation r²+ar+b=0 gives roots. Real distinct roots give y=C₁e^(r₁x)+C₂e^(r₂x); repeated roots add x e^(rx); complex roots r = α ± iβ give e^(αx)(C₁ cos βx + C₂ sin βx). For nonconstant coefficients, use series or numerical methods. A system x′ = Ax couples unknowns; eigenvalues of A give modes, and stability depends on their real parts.

sections.heading: Transforms and series
sections.text: Laplace transform turns t-functions into s-functions: L{y} = Y(s) = ∫₀∞ e^(−st) y(t) dt. Then L{y′}=sY(s)−y(0), so initial value problems become algebra. The transform is linear: L{af+bg}=aL{f}+bL{g}. Series solutions assume y=Σ aₙxⁿ; substitute and match powers to find coefficients. This works near ordinary points and, with care, at regular singular points.

sections.heading: Simple models
sections.text: Simple models use these equations. Radioactive decay or drug clearance: dN/dt = −kN, giving N=N₀e^(−kt). Logistic growth: dP/dt = rP(1−P/K), with carrying capacity K. The logistic equation is nonlinear and usually solved by separation. A damped spring obeys m y″ + c y′ + k y = 0. Two connected compartments give a linear system. Always state units and check the solution against the initial condition.

keyPoints: First-order linear equations y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) are solved with μ = e^(∫P dx).
Separable equations are solved by separating variables and integrating both sides.
For constant-coefficient second-order equations, solve r² + ar + b = 0 to get the form of y.
A linear system x′ = Ax is understood through the eigenvalues of A.
Laplace transforms use L{y′} = sY(s) − y(0) to turn initial value problems into algebra.
Series solutions substitute y = Σ aₙxⁿ and match coefficients.

en.title: Real analysis: rigorous foundations
en.short: Definitions and proofs for limits, series, continuity, derivatives, Riemann integrals and uniform convergence.

sections.heading: Limits and sequences
sections.text:
Real analysis replaces informal ideas of closeness with inequalities. A sequence (aₙ) converges to L if for every ε > 0 there is N such that |aₙ − L| < ε for all n > N. A Cauchy sequence satisfies |aₙ − aₘ| < ε for all large m, n; in R this is equivalent to convergence. A series Σaₙ converges when its partial sums Sₙ = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ converge. Comparison and ratio tests must be proved from these definitions.

Example: show aₙ = (2n + 1)/(n + 3) → 2. Then |aₙ − 2| = |(2n + 1 − 2n − 6)/(n + 3)| = 5/(n + 3). Given ε > 0, take N > 5/ε. For n > N, 5/(n + 3) < 5/n < ε. So the definition holds.

sections.heading: Continuity and derivatives
sections.text: Continuity at c means: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |x − c| < δ implies |f(x) − f(c)| < ε. Equivalently, f(xₙ) → f(c) for every sequence xₙ → c. The derivative is f′(c) = lim (h→0) [f(c+h) − f(c)]/h when this limit exists. Proofs use these definitions. The mean value theorem links the sign of f′ to monotonicity and gives Taylor’s theorem with remainder under stated conditions.

sections.heading: Riemann integral
sections.text: The Riemann integral is built from partitions. For a bounded f on [a,b], define lower and upper sums using inf and sup on each subinterval. f is Riemann integrable if the infimum of upper sums equals the supremum of lower sums; then the common value is ∫_a^b f. Continuous functions on closed bounded intervals are integrable. The fundamental theorem says if F′ = f and f is integrable, then ∫_a^b f = F(b) − F(a).

sections.heading: Uniform convergence
sections.text: Pointwise convergence of fₙ to f means fₙ(x) → f(x) for each x. Uniform convergence means sup over x of |fₙ(x) − f(x)| → 0. Uniform limits preserve continuity and integrability, and allow swapping limit and integral. Derivatives need extra care: uniform convergence of fₙ′ plus convergence at one point gives f′ = lim fₙ′. Counterexamples show pointwise convergence alone is not enough.

keyPoints: Convergence: for every ε > 0 there is N such that n > N implies |aₙ − L| < ε.
Continuity at c: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |x − c| < δ implies |f(x) − f(c)| < ε.
Derivative: f′(c) = lim (h→0) [f(c+h) − f(c)]/h when the limit exists.
Riemann integrability means the supremum of the lower sums equals the infimum of the upper sums; the integral is that common value.
Uniform convergence means sup over x of |fₙ(x) − f(x)| → 0, and it preserves continuity and integrability.
Uniform convergence of derivatives plus convergence at one point allows f′ = lim fₙ′.

en.title: Abstract algebra: groups, rings and fields
en.short: Groups, subgroups, homomorphisms, quotient groups, rings, ideals, fields and simple field extensions.

sections.heading: Groups and subgroups
sections.text:
A group is a set G with an associative operation, an identity e, and inverses for every element. It is abelian if the operation is commutative. A subgroup H is a subset that is itself a group under the same operation; it must contain e and be closed under products and inverses.

Example: Z/6Z = {0,1,2,3,4,5} under addition mod 6 is a group. H = {0,2,4} is a subgroup: 2+4=0, 4+4=2, and each element has its inverse in H.

sections.heading: Homomorphisms and quotients
sections.text:
A homomorphism φ:G→H satisfies φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b). Its kernel ker φ = {g∈G: φ(g)=e_H} is a normal subgroup, and its image is a subgroup. For a normal subgroup N, the cosets gN form the quotient group G/N under (gN)(hN)=ghN. The first isomorphism theorem says G/ker φ is isomorphic to im φ.

Example: φ:Z→Z/6Z, φ(n)=2n mod 6. The kernel is 3Z and the image is {0,2,4}, so Z/3Z is isomorphic to {0,2,4}.

sections.heading: Rings and ideals
sections.text:
A ring R has addition making it an abelian group and multiplication that is associative and distributes over addition. If multiplication is commutative and there is a multiplicative identity 1 ≠ 0, it is a commutative ring with unity. An ideal I is an additive subgroup with rI ⊆ I and Ir ⊆ I for all r ∈ R. Then R/I is a quotient ring.

Example: in Z, the multiples of 6 form the ideal 6Z, so Z/6Z is a quotient ring. It is not a field: 2 × 3 = 0 mod 6.

sections.heading: Fields and extensions
sections.text:
A field is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. Q, R and C are fields; Z/pZ is a field exactly when p is prime.

A field extension K/F means F is a subfield of K. Its degree [K:F] is the dimension of K over F. Example: Q(√2) = {a+b√2 : a,b∈Q}. It is a field: (a+b√2)(c+d√2) = (ac+2bd)+(ad+bc)√2, and for a+b√2 ≠ 0 the inverse is (a−b√2)/(a²−2b²). Since 1 and √2 form a basis, [Q(√2):Q] = 2.

keyPoints: A group is a set with an associative operation, an identity and inverses; a subgroup is closed under the operation and inverses.
A homomorphism preserves the operation: φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b); its kernel is a normal subgroup.
The first isomorphism theorem: G/ker φ is isomorphic to im φ.
An ideal I allows the quotient ring R/I; in Z the ideal 6Z gives Z/6Z.
A field is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 where every nonzero element has an inverse; Z/pZ is a field when p is prime.
For a field extension K/F, the degree [K:F] is the dimension of K over F; [Q(√2):Q] = 2.

en.title: Complex analysis: analytic functions, integrals and residues
en.short: Analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations, contour integrals, Cauchy’s theorem, residues and conformal maps.

sections.heading: Analytic functions
sections.text:
A function f is analytic (also called holomorphic) at a point if it has a complex derivative on some open disc around that point. Write f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y), with u and v real.

If f is analytic, u and v satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations: u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x. With continuous partial derivatives, these equations are also sufficient for analyticity.

Example: f(z) = z², so u = x² − y² and v = 2xy. Then u_x = 2x = v_y and u_y = −2y = −v_x, so f is analytic everywhere.

sections.heading: Contour integration
sections.text:
A contour is a piecewise smooth path in the plane. The integral of f along a contour γ is written ∫γ f(z) dz. You compute it by parametrising: put z = γ(t), so dz = γ′(t) dt, then integrate over t.

Example: integrate f(z) = z along the straight line from 0 to 1 + i. Take z = t(1+i) with 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, so dz = (1+i) dt.
∫ = ∫₀¹ t(1+i)(1+i) dt = (1+i)² ÷ 2 = 2i ÷ 2 = i.

sections.heading: Cauchy’s theorem
sections.text:
Cauchy’s theorem: if f is analytic on a simply connected domain (one with no holes) and γ is a closed contour inside it, then ∮γ f(z) dz = 0.

Cauchy’s integral formula: if a lies inside γ, then f(a) = (1 ÷ 2πi) ∮γ f(z) ÷ (z − a) dz. So the values of an analytic function inside are fixed by its values on the boundary.

Example: ∮ over |z| = 2 of e^z ÷ (z − 1) dz = 2πi e, because a = 1 lies inside the circle.

sections.heading: Residues and mapping
sections.text:
The residue of f at an isolated singularity a is the coefficient a₋₁ in its Laurent series. The residue theorem says ∮γ f(z) dz = 2πi times the sum of residues inside γ. At a simple pole, Res = lim as z → a of (z − a)f(z).

Example: ∮ over |z| = 1 of 1 ÷ z dz = 2πi, since the residue at 0 is 1.

A map is conformal where it is analytic and its derivative is nonzero; it preserves angles between curves. Möbius maps (az + b) ÷ (cz + d), with ad − bc ≠ 0, send circles and lines to circles and lines.

keyPoints: f is analytic where it has a complex derivative on an open disc.
Cauchy-Riemann equations: u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x.
Cauchy’s theorem: ∮γ f(z) dz = 0 for f analytic on a simply connected domain.
Cauchy’s integral formula: f(a) = (1 ÷ 2πi) ∮γ f(z) ÷ (z − a) dz.
Residue theorem: ∮γ f(z) dz = 2πi Σ residues inside γ.
A conformal map is analytic with nonzero derivative and preserves angles.

en.title: Probability theory: axioms to limit theorems
en.short: Axioms, random variables, distributions, expectation, independence, generating functions and limit theorems.

sections.heading: Axioms and variables
sections.text: A probability space is a sample space Ω, a sigma-algebra F (a collection of events closed under complements and countable unions) and a probability measure P on F. P satisfies P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A; P(Ω) = 1; and for disjoint events A1, A2, ..., P(∪Ai) = Σ P(Ai). These are Kolmogorov’s axioms. A random variable X is a function from Ω to the real numbers such that events like {X ≤ x} belong to F.

sections.heading: Distributions and expectation
sections.text:
The distribution function is F(x) = P(X ≤ x). It is non-decreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 and 1. For discrete X, P(X = x) is the probability mass function; for continuous X, a density f satisfies F(x) = ∫ from −∞ to x f(t) dt. Expectation is E(X) = Σ x P(X = x) or ∫ x f(x) dx. Variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

Example: a fair die has E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) ÷ 6 = 3.5 and Var(X) = 91 ÷ 6 − 3.5² = 35 ÷ 12 ≈ 2.917.

sections.heading: Independence and generating functions
sections.text: Events A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Random variables X and Y are independent if P(X ≤ x, Y ≤ y) = P(X ≤ x)P(Y ≤ y) for all x, y. The probability generating function of a non-negative integer-valued X is G(s) = E(s^X). The moment generating function is M(t) = E(e^(tX)), where it exists. For independent X and Y, M(X+Y)(t) = M(X)(t)M(Y)(t).

sections.heading: Limit theorems
sections.text: The weak law of large numbers says that for independent, identically distributed X1, X2, ... with finite mean μ, the sample mean converges in probability to μ, meaning the chance of a large gap tends to zero. The strong law gives almost sure convergence. The central limit theorem says that if the Xi have finite mean μ and variance σ², then (X1 + ... + Xn − nμ) ÷ (σ√n) tends in distribution to the standard normal N(0,1).

keyPoints: Kolmogorov’s axioms: P(A) ≥ 0, P(Ω) = 1 and P(∪Ai) = Σ P(Ai) for disjoint events.
The distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is non-decreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 and 1.
Expectation is E(X) = Σ x P(X = x) or ∫ x f(x) dx, and Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
Events A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); independent variables have M(X+Y)(t) = M(X)(t)M(Y)(t).
The law of large numbers makes the sample mean approach the population mean μ.
The central limit theorem makes (ΣXi − nμ) ÷ (σ√n) approach N(0,1).

en.title: Mathematical statistics: estimation, testing and models
en.short: Sampling distributions, maximum likelihood, confidence intervals, tests, regression and ANOVA.

sections.heading: Sampling distributions
sections.text: A statistic such as the sample mean is random. Its sampling distribution is the distribution it would have over repeated samples of size n. The standard error is its standard deviation; for a mean it is σ/√n, estimated by s/√n. The central limit theorem says that for large n the sample mean is approximately normal whatever the population, provided the variance is finite. For small samples from a normal population with unknown σ, use the t distribution.

sections.heading: Point estimation
sections.text: An estimator is a rule for guessing a parameter; an estimate is the value it gives. Good estimators are unbiased, consistent and efficient. The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) is the parameter value that makes the observed data most likely. Maximise the likelihood L(θ), or usually its logarithm. Example: with n independent Bernoulli trials and x successes, L(p)=p^x(1−p)^(n−x). Setting d/dp log L = x/p − (n−x)/(1−p) = 0 gives p̂=x/n.

sections.heading: Intervals and tests
sections.text: A confidence interval is a range with a stated long-run coverage. For a mean with known σ, x̄ ± z σ/√n; with unknown σ use s and a t critical value. Example: n=25, x̄=52, s=10, so SE=10/5=2. Since σ is unknown, use t with 24 degrees of freedom: a 95% interval is 52 ± 2.064×2 = (47.87, 56.13). A hypothesis test sets H0 and H1, computes a test statistic, and reports a p-value: the probability, if H0 is true, of a result at least as extreme. Reject H0 when p is below the chosen significance level α. Errors are Type I (reject a true H0) and Type II (fail to reject a false H0).

sections.heading: Regression and ANOVA
sections.text: Simple linear regression models y = β0 + β1x + ε. Least squares chooses b1 = Σ(xi−x̄)(yi−ȳ) ÷ Σ(xi−x̄)² and b0 = ȳ − b1x̄. ANOVA compares several group means by splitting total variation into between-group and within-group sums of squares; the F statistic is MSbetween ÷ MSwithin. It assumes independent normal observations with equal variances.

keyPoints: Sampling distribution: the distribution of a statistic over repeated samples; SE(x̄)=σ/√n.
MLE maximises L(θ) or log L(θ); for Bernoulli data p̂=x/n.
A 95% CI for a mean with known σ is x̄ ± 1.96σ/√n; use t when σ is unknown and n is small.
A p-value is the probability under H0 of a result at least as extreme; compare it with α.
Simple linear regression: y = β0 + β1x + ε, with b1 = Σ(xi−x̄)(yi−ȳ) ÷ Σ(xi−x̄)².
One-way ANOVA uses F = MSbetween ÷ MSwithin and assumes independent normal groups with equal variances.

en.title: Numerical analysis: approximation, error and algorithms
en.short: Floating-point error, root finding, interpolation, integration, linear systems, eigenvalues and ODE methods.

sections.heading: Errors and floating point
sections.text:
Computers store real numbers in floating point: a sign, a significand (the main digits) and an exponent. Rounding gives absolute error |x − x̂| and relative error |x − x̂| ÷ |x| for x ≠ 0. Machine epsilon is the gap between 1 and the next representable number.

A problem is ill-conditioned if small input changes cause large output changes; an algorithm is unstable if it magnifies rounding error. Compare errors with a tolerance, not exact equality.

sections.heading: Roots and interpolation
sections.text:
Root finding solves f(x) = 0. Bisection halves a sign-changing interval and converges linearly. Newton’s method uses x(k+1) = x(k) − f(x(k)) ÷ f′(x(k)) and converges quadratically near a simple root, but can fail.

Interpolation fits a polynomial through n + 1 data points; Lagrange form is standard. High-degree interpolation can oscillate (Runge phenomenon). Example: solve x² − 2 = 0 from x0 = 1.5. x1 = 1.5 − 0.25 ÷ 3 = 1.4166667. x2 = 1.4166667 − 0.0069444 ÷ 2.8333334 = 1.4142157.

sections.heading: Linear systems and eigenvalues
sections.text:
Linear systems Ax = b are solved directly by Gaussian elimination with row swaps, cost O(n³), or iteratively by Jacobi or Gauss-Seidel, which converge when the diagonal entries dominate.

Eigenvalues can be found by power iteration for the dominant eigenvalue, and by the QR algorithm for all eigenvalues. Condition number measures sensitivity of the solution to data errors.

sections.heading: Integration and ODEs
sections.text:
Numerical integration approximates ∫ f(x) dx by weighted function values. Trapezium rule error is O(h²); Simpson’s rule is O(h⁴) for smooth functions.

For y′ = f(x,y), Euler’s method steps y(k+1) = y(k) + h f(x(k), y(k)) with local error O(h²). Runge-Kutta methods, especially fourth-order RK4, give higher accuracy. Smaller h reduces truncation error but increases rounding and cost.

keyPoints: Floating-point error is measured by absolute error |x − x̂| and relative error |x − x̂| ÷ |x|; machine epsilon is the gap between 1 and the next representable number.
Bisection converges linearly; Newton’s method uses x(k+1) = x(k) − f(x(k)) ÷ f′(x(k)) and converges quadratically near a simple root.
Lagrange interpolation fits a polynomial through n + 1 points, but high degree can cause Runge oscillation.
Gaussian elimination with row swaps solves Ax = b in O(n³); Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel are iterative alternatives when the diagonal entries dominate.
Trapezium rule error is O(h²) and Simpson’s rule error is O(h⁴) for smooth integrands.
Euler’s method has local error O(h²), fourth-order Runge-Kutta is more accurate, power iteration finds the dominant eigenvalue and QR finds all eigenvalues.

en.title: Discrete mathematics and combinatorics
en.short: Counting, permutations, inclusion-exclusion, pigeonhole, recurrences and generating functions.

sections.heading: Counting principles
sections.text: The product rule says that if a task has m choices at one stage and n at the next, it has m × n ways in all. The sum rule says that if two cases cannot happen together, their counts add. These rules count ordered choices; for unordered selections use combinations. Example: a student chooses one of 4 main dishes and one of 3 drinks, giving 4 × 3 = 12 meals.

sections.heading: Permutations and combinations
sections.text: A permutation is an ordered arrangement. The number of ways to arrange r objects chosen from n distinct objects is P(n,r) = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination is an unordered selection: C(n,r) = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!), also written (n choose r). Example: from 8 students, the number of 3-person committees is C(8,3) = 8! ÷ (3!5!) = 56. If the three are given distinct roles, the count is P(8,3) = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336.

sections.heading: Inclusion-exclusion and pigeonhole
sections.text: For two overlapping sets, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. For three, subtract the pairwise intersections and add back the triple intersection. The pigeonhole principle says that if n items are placed in k boxes and n > k, some box holds at least two items. More generally, some box holds at least n ÷ k rounded up. Example: 13 people have birthdays in 12 months, so two share a month.

sections.heading: Recurrences and generating functions
sections.text: A recurrence relation defines a sequence by earlier terms, such as a_n = a_{n−1} + a_{n−2} with a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1. A generating function turns a sequence into a power series, G(x) = Σ a_n x^n. For that recurrence, G(x) = x ÷ (1 − x − x²). Example: a_2 = 1, a_3 = 2, a_4 = 3. Generating functions solve recurrences by algebra on series.

keyPoints: Product rule: if stages have m and n choices, total is m × n; sum rule adds disjoint cases.
P(n,r) = n! ÷ (n − r)! counts ordered arrangements; C(n,r) = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!) counts unordered selections.
Inclusion-exclusion: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|, with alternating signs for more sets.
Pigeonhole: n items in k boxes with n > k force a shared box; some box has at least n ÷ k rounded up.
A recurrence defines terms from earlier ones; a generating function G(x) = Σ a_n x^n encodes the whole sequence.

en.title: Graph theory: structure, paths and colouring
en.short: Graphs, digraphs, trees, connectivity, Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs, colouring, matching and planar graphs.

sections.heading: Graphs and digraphs
sections.text: A graph G = (V, E) has vertices V and edges E joining pairs. A simple graph has no loops or repeated edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of incident edges. The handshaking lemma says the sum of all degrees equals 2|E|. A digraph has directed edges, so each vertex has an indegree and an outdegree. Example: a triangle has degrees 2, 2, 2; their sum is 6 = 2 × 3.

sections.heading: Trees and connectivity
sections.text: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. A tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges, and any two vertices are joined by exactly one path. A graph is connected if a path joins every pair of vertices. Its components are its maximal connected subgraphs. Removing a cut vertex increases the number of components. Every connected graph contains a spanning tree, a tree using all its vertices.

sections.heading: Eulerian, Hamiltonian, colouring
sections.text: An Eulerian circuit uses every edge exactly once and returns to its start. A connected graph has one if and only if every vertex has even degree. An Eulerian trail uses every edge once and exists when exactly zero or two vertices have odd degree. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once. No simple necessary and sufficient condition is known. A colouring gives adjacent vertices different colours; the least number needed is the chromatic number. A triangle needs 3 colours; a 4-cycle needs 2.

sections.heading: Matching and planarity
sections.text: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints; a perfect matching covers every vertex. In a bipartite graph with parts X and Y, Hall’s theorem says a matching covering X exists if and only if every subset S of X has at least |S| neighbours. A planar graph can be drawn in the plane without crossing edges. For a connected planar graph, v − e + f = 2, where f counts faces including the outer face. Example: a cube has v = 8, e = 12, f = 6, and 8 − 12 + 6 = 2.

keyPoints: Handshaking lemma: the sum of all vertex degrees is 2|E|.
A tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices.
A connected graph is Eulerian exactly when every vertex has even degree.
No simple necessary and sufficient test for Hamiltonian cycles is known.
Hall’s theorem gives the condition for a matching covering one side of a bipartite graph.
For a connected planar graph, v − e + f = 2.

en.title: Elementary number theory
en.short: Divisibility, primes, gcd, congruences, the Chinese remainder theorem, quadratic residues and Diophantine equations.

sections.heading: Divisibility and primes
sections.text: An integer a divides b, written a | b, if b = ak for some integer k. Division with remainder gives b = aq + r with 0 ≤ r < |a|. A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. Every integer greater than 1 factors into primes uniquely up to order (fundamental theorem of arithmetic). Euclid’s lemma: if p is prime and p | ab, then p | a or p | b.

sections.heading: GCD and congruences
sections.text: The greatest common divisor gcd(a,b) is the largest positive integer dividing both. Euclid’s algorithm uses gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,r), where a = bq + r. If gcd(a,b) = 1, a and b are coprime. Bézout’s identity: integers x,y exist with ax + by = gcd(a,b). A congruence a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a − b. Congruences add, subtract and multiply. Division by c is allowed only when gcd(c,n) = 1. The congruence ax ≡ b (mod n) is solvable exactly when gcd(a,n) divides b.

sections.heading: CRT and residues
sections.text: The Chinese remainder theorem: if n1, ..., nk are pairwise coprime, the system x ≡ ai (mod ni) has one solution modulo N = n1...nk. Example: x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5). The first congruence gives 2,5,8,11,14; 8 satisfies the second, so x ≡ 8 (mod 15). A quadratic residue modulo n is a square a² mod n. For odd prime p, the Legendre symbol (a/p) is 1 for a nonzero square, −1 otherwise, and 0 when p | a. Euler’s criterion: a^((p−1)/2) ≡ (a/p) (mod p).

sections.heading: Diophantine equations
sections.text: A Diophantine equation asks for integer solutions. The linear equation ax + by = c is solvable exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c. 6x + 9y = 15, divide by 3: 2x + 3y = 5. A solution is x = 1, y = 1. All solutions: x = 1 + 3t, y = 1 − 2t.

keyPoints: a | b means b = ak for some integer k.
Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation up to order.
Euclid’s algorithm: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,r) when a = bq + r.
ax ≡ b (mod n) is solvable exactly when gcd(a,n) divides b.
The CRT gives a unique solution modulo the product when the moduli are pairwise coprime.
For odd prime p, Euler’s criterion is a^((p−1)/2) ≡ (a/p) (mod p).

en.title: Topology: spaces, continuity and shape
en.short: Metric and topological spaces, open and closed sets, continuity, compactness, connectedness and homeomorphism.

sections.heading: Spaces and open sets
sections.text: A metric space is a set X with a distance d(x,y) that is zero only when x = y, is symmetric, and obeys d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,z). The open ball B(x,r) is the set of points with d(x,y) < r. A subset U is open if every point of U has an open ball inside U. A topology on X is a collection of open sets containing the empty set and X, closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions. Closed means the complement is open. In R with d(x,y) = |x − y|, (0,1) is open and [0,1] is closed.

sections.heading: Continuity and homeomorphism
sections.text: A map f: X → Y between topological spaces is continuous if the preimage of every open set in Y is open in X. For metric spaces this is equivalent, at every point a, to the usual ε-δ condition: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that d(x,a) < δ implies d(f(x),f(a)) < ε. A homeomorphism is a bijection f that is continuous and whose inverse is continuous. Homeomorphic spaces have the same topological properties. For example, f(x) = tan(π(x − 1/2)) maps (0,1) homeomorphically onto R, with f(1/4) = −1, f(1/2) = 0 and f(3/4) = 1.

sections.heading: Compactness and connectedness
sections.text: A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. In R^n, the Heine-Borel theorem says a subset is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. The continuous image of a compact space is compact. A space is connected if it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets. Intervals in R are connected, and the continuous image of a connected space is connected; this gives the intermediate value theorem. [0,1] is compact and connected, while (0,1) is connected but not compact. [0,1] and (0,1) are therefore not homeomorphic.

keyPoints: Open sets are the basic objects of a topology; closed sets are their complements.
A map is continuous exactly when preimages of open sets are open.
A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse; homeomorphic spaces share topological properties.
Compact means every open cover has a finite subcover; in R^n this is equivalent to closed and bounded.
Connected means the space cannot split into two disjoint nonempty open pieces.
Continuous images of compact or connected spaces remain compact or connected.

en.title: Partial differential equations: characteristics and Fourier methods
en.short: First-order characteristics, classification, heat, wave and Laplace equations, separation of variables and Fourier series.

sections.heading: First-order equations
sections.text:
A first-order linear partial differential equation (PDE) has the form a u_x + b u_y = c, where u(x,y) is unknown and subscripts mean partial derivatives. Its characteristic curves satisfy dx/a = dy/b = du/c. Along a characteristic, u obeys an ordinary differential equation, so the PDE reduces to ODEs.

Example: u_x + u_y = 0 with u(x,0)=f(x). dx/1 = dy/1 gives x − y constant; u is constant on each such line, so u=f(x − y). Check: u_x=f′, u_y=−f′, so u_x+u_y=0, and u(x,0)=f(x).

sections.heading: Second-order classification
sections.text:
For A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + lower-order terms = 0, compute D=B²−4AC. D>0 is hyperbolic, D=0 parabolic, D<0 elliptic. Some books write the cross term as 2B u_xy; then use B²−AC. The type controls which data are appropriate and how disturbances travel.

Example: u_xx−u_yy=0 has D=4, hyperbolic; u_xx+u_yy=0 has D=−4, elliptic; u_t−u_xx=0 is parabolic.

sections.heading: Three model equations
sections.text:
The heat equation u_t=κu_xx models diffusion; κ>0 is diffusivity. The wave equation u_tt=c²u_xx models vibration; c is wave speed. Laplace’s equation u_xx+u_yy=0 models steady states. Each needs boundary conditions, and heat and wave also need initial conditions.

The heat equation smooths data and has infinite propagation speed in the model; the wave equation carries signals at speed c; Laplace solutions are determined by boundary values.

sections.heading: Separation and Fourier
sections.text:
Separation of variables tries u=X(x)T(t) on a rectangle or interval. Substitution gives one side depending on x and the other on t, so both equal a constant. Boundary conditions select allowed constants and sine or cosine modes. The solution is a Fourier series whose coefficients match the initial condition.

Example: heat equation on 0<x<L with u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0 and u(x,0)=sin(πx/L). Then u=sin(πx/L)e^{−κπ²t/L²}. Check: u_t=−κπ²/L² u and u_xx=−π²/L² u, so u_t=κu_xx; ends vanish; at t=0 it equals the initial sine.

keyPoints: First-order linear PDE a u_x + b u_y = c is solved along characteristics dx/a = dy/b = du/c.
For A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + ... =0, D=B²−4AC: D>0 hyperbolic, D=0 parabolic, D<0 elliptic.
Heat u_t=κu_xx, wave u_tt=c²u_xx and Laplace u_xx+u_yy=0 are the three model second-order equations.
Separation of variables writes u=X(x)T(t), giving ODEs and allowed modes from boundary conditions.
Fourier series match initial data; for zero ends the heat modes are sin(nπx/L)e^{−κn²π²t/L²}.
The heat equation smooths data, the wave equation carries signals at speed c, and Laplace solutions are fixed by boundary values.

en.title: Optimisation and operations research
en.short: Linear programming, simplex, duality, transport and assignment, nonlinear optimisation and dynamic programming.

sections.heading: Linear programming
sections.text:
Linear programming (LP) maximises or minimises a linear objective subject to linear inequalities. The feasible region is convex, so an optimum lies at a vertex.

Example: maximise P = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x + 2y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0. Vertices give P = 0 at (0,0), 12 at (4,0), 6 at (0,3) and 10 at (2,2). The maximum is 12 at (4,0).

sections.heading: Simplex and duality
sections.text:
The simplex method starts at a feasible vertex and moves along an edge to a better vertex until none improves. Tableaux use slack variables.

Every LP has a dual. For max c·x with Ax ≤ b and x ≥ 0, the dual is min b·y with A^T y ≥ c and y ≥ 0. Weak duality gives c·x ≤ b·y; strong duality makes the optima equal. Dual variables are shadow prices, the optimum change per unit rise in a right side.

sections.heading: Transport and assignment
sections.text:
A transportation problem ships one good from sources with supplies to destinations with demands at least cost. It is an LP with one variable per route. If total supply does not equal total demand, add a dummy source or destination. The northwest-corner rule gives a starting plan; stepping-stone or MODI improves it.

An assignment problem matches each worker to one job at least cost. It is a transportation problem with unit supplies and demands; the Hungarian method solves it.

sections.heading: Nonlinear and dynamic
sections.text:
Nonlinear optimisation allows curved objectives or constraints. A local optimum beats nearby feasible points; a global optimum beats all. For convex problems a local optimum is global, and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions generalise Lagrange multipliers to inequalities.

Dynamic programming solves a problem in stages, storing the best value for each state. It uses optimal substructure: an optimal policy contains optimal policies for later stages. The Bellman recurrence expresses one stage’s best value through the next.

keyPoints: An LP maximises or minimises c·x subject to Ax ≤ b and x ≥ 0; if an optimum exists, a vertex is optimal.
The simplex method moves from vertex to vertex along improving edges, using slack variables and pivot operations.
The dual of max c·x with Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0 is min b·y with A^T y ≥ c, y ≥ 0; strong duality makes their optima equal.
Dual variables are shadow prices: they show the change in the optimum per unit rise in a constraint’s right side.
Transportation and assignment problems are special LPs; the Hungarian method solves assignment problems.
For convex nonlinear problems KKT conditions generalise Lagrange multipliers and are sufficient under mild conditions; dynamic programming uses the Bellman recurrence over states and stages.

en.title: Mathematical modelling
en.short: Covers the modelling cycle, dimensional analysis, deterministic and stochastic models, and validation.

sections.heading: The modelling cycle
sections.text: Modelling starts with a real question, such as how fast an infection spreads. You choose variables, make assumptions, and write equations or rules. Then you solve or simulate, compare the output with data, and revise the assumptions. The loop is the modelling cycle. A model is a purposeful simplification, not a copy of reality. State every assumption, because it limits what the model can claim.

sections.heading: Dimensions and scaling
sections.text: Dimensional analysis checks that every term has the same units. A dimensionless group has no units, such as a ratio of two lengths. Scaling asks how output changes when inputs are multiplied. For a pendulum, period T can depend only on length L and gravity g. The only combination with units of time is T = k√(L/g), where k is dimensionless. If L rises from 1.00 m to 4.00 m, T rises by √4 = 2, so the period doubles. With k = 2π, T = 2π√(1.00/9.81) = 2.006 s, and for 4.00 m it is 4.012 s.

sections.heading: Deterministic and stochastic
sections.text: A deterministic model gives one outcome for given inputs. A falling stone or a simple SIR (susceptible, infected, recovered) epidemic model is deterministic. A stochastic model includes randomness: the outcome is a probability distribution, not a single number. A clinic queue with random arrivals is stochastic. Build deterministic models from balance laws, such as conservation of people or mass. Build stochastic models from transition probabilities or random variables. Both need parameters, and both can be simulated.

sections.heading: Validation and cases
sections.text: Validation tests whether a model is fit for its purpose. Check units, compare predictions with independent data, and test sensitivity: how much outputs change when a parameter changes. Calibration fits parameters to data, but a calibrated model can still fail on new data. Case studies include epidemic control, predator and prey populations, traffic flow, and clinic queues. In each, the model informs decisions but never replaces judgement.

keyPoints: The modelling cycle is question, assumptions, model, solution, comparison with data, revision.
Dimensional analysis requires every term in an equation to have the same units; dimensionless groups have no units.
For a pendulum, dimensional analysis gives T = k√(L/g), and scaling length by 4 multiplies the period by 2.
Deterministic models give one outcome for given inputs; stochastic models give a probability distribution.
Validate a model by checking units, comparing with independent data, and testing sensitivity to parameters.
Calibration fits parameters to data, but a calibrated model can still fail on new data.

en.title: Measure theory and integration
en.short: Sigma-algebras, measures, measurable functions, Lebesgue integration, convergence, products and Radon-Nikodym.

sections.heading: Sigma-algebras and measures
sections.text: A sigma-algebra on a set X is a family of subsets containing X, closed under complements and countable unions. Its members are measurable. A measure μ assigns a value in [0,∞] to measurable sets, with μ(∅)=0 and countable additivity: for disjoint A_n, μ(∪A_n)=Σμ(A_n). A measure space is (X, Σ, μ). Lebesgue measure λ on R extends length: λ([a,b])=b−a. A null set has measure zero; a property holds almost everywhere if it fails only on a null set.

sections.heading: Measurable functions
sections.text: f: X→R is measurable if f⁻¹((a,∞)) is measurable for every real a, equivalently if every Borel set has measurable preimage. The Borel sigma-algebra is generated by open sets. Sums, products and pointwise limits of measurable functions are measurable. A nonnegative simple function takes finitely many values: s=Σ c_i 1_{A_i} with disjoint A_i. Its integral is Σ c_i μ(A_i).

sections.heading: Lebesgue integral
sections.text: For nonnegative measurable f, ∫f dμ = sup ∫s dμ over simple 0≤s≤f. For general f, split into positive and negative parts when at least one integral is finite. If ∫|f|<∞, f is integrable. The integral is linear and monotone. Example: on [0,1] with λ, let s=2 on [0,1/4] and 3 on (1/4,1/2], zero elsewhere. ∫s dλ = 2(1/4)+3(1/4)=1.25. The integral agrees with the Riemann integral for Riemann-integrable functions on bounded intervals.

sections.heading: Convergence and products
sections.text: Monotone convergence: if 0≤f_n↑f, then ∫f_n→∫f. Dominated convergence: if f_n→f and |f_n|≤g with ∫g<∞, then ∫f_n→∫f. A measure space is sigma-finite if X is a countable union of measurable sets of finite measure. For sigma-finite spaces, product measure μ×ν is unique with (μ×ν)(A×B)=μ(A)ν(B); Tonelli and Fubini justify swapping integrals. Tonelli applies to nonnegative functions; Fubini needs integrability. If ν≪μ (ν(A)=0 whenever μ(A)=0) and both are sigma-finite, Radon-Nikodym gives a density f with ν(A)=∫_A f dμ for all measurable A. The density is unique almost everywhere and written dν/dμ.

keyPoints: A sigma-algebra is closed under complements and countable unions; a measure is countably additive with μ(∅)=0.
Measurable functions have measurable preimages of Borel sets, and pointwise limits of measurable functions are measurable.
For nonnegative measurable f, ∫f dμ = sup ∫s dμ over simple 0≤s≤f.
Monotone convergence: if 0≤f_n↑f then ∫f_n→∫f; dominated convergence: if |f_n|≤g with ∫g<∞ then ∫f_n→∫f.
For sigma-finite measures, μ×ν is determined by (μ×ν)(A×B)=μ(A)ν(B), and Tonelli and Fubini justify iterated integrals.
If ν≪μ and both are sigma-finite, Radon-Nikodym gives f=dν/dμ with ν(A)=∫_A f dμ.

en.title: Functional analysis: spaces, operators and spectra
en.short: Banach and Hilbert spaces, bounded operators, duals, the big theorems and basic spectral theory.

sections.heading: Banach and Hilbert spaces
sections.text:
A normed space has a norm ||x|| that gives length and distance d(x,y)=||x−y||. It is a Banach space if every Cauchy sequence converges in the space. A Hilbert space is a Banach space whose norm comes from an inner product: ||x||=√⟨x,x⟩.

Example: R^n with the Euclidean norm is a Hilbert space. The space C[0,1] of continuous functions with the sup norm is Banach but not Hilbert, because its norm does not satisfy the parallelogram law.

sections.heading: Operators and duals
sections.text:
A linear operator T:X→Y is bounded if ||T||=sup{||Tx||:||x||≤1} is finite. For linear maps, bounded is equivalent to continuous. The dual space X* is the Banach space of bounded linear functionals f:X→F, with norm ||f||=sup{|f(x)|:||x||≤1}.

Example: on R² with the Euclidean norm, f(x,y)=2x+3y has ||f||=√(2²+3²)=√13≈3.606, since |2x+3y|≤√13√(x²+y²).

sections.heading: Three big theorems
sections.text:
The Hahn-Banach theorem says that a bounded linear functional on a subspace of a normed space extends to the whole space with the same norm. It gives separation of convex sets and shows that X* is rich enough to separate points.

The open mapping theorem says that a bounded linear surjection between Banach spaces maps open sets to open sets. The closed graph theorem says that a linear map between Banach spaces whose graph is closed is bounded. The inverse mapping theorem follows from the open mapping theorem.

sections.heading: Basic spectral theory
sections.text:
For T in B(X) on a complex Banach space, the spectrum σ(T) is the set of λ for which T−λI has no bounded inverse. Its complement is the resolvent set. The spectrum is nonempty, compact and lies in |λ|≤||T||. Eigenvalues belong to σ(T), but σ(T) may contain non-eigenvalues.

Example: T(z,w)=(2z,3w) on C² has ||T||=3 and σ(T)={2,3}; T−λI is invertible exactly when λ≠2,3. The spectral radius is r(T)=lim ||T^n||^(1/n).

keyPoints: A Banach space is complete in its norm; a Hilbert space has a norm from an inner product.
For a bounded linear operator, ||T|| = sup{||Tx|| : ||x|| ≤ 1}, and boundedness is equivalent to continuity.
The dual norm is ||f|| = sup{|f(x)| : ||x|| ≤ 1}.
Hahn-Banach extends a bounded linear functional from a subspace to the whole normed space without increasing its norm.
A bounded linear surjection between Banach spaces is open, and a closed graph implies boundedness.
The spectrum σ(T) is the set of λ for which T − λI has no bounded inverse; the spectral radius satisfies r(T) = lim ||T^n||^(1/n).

en.title: Stochastic processes
en.short: Markov chains, Poisson processes, Brownian motion, martingales, stationarity and applications.

sections.heading: Markov chains
sections.text:
A Markov chain is a sequence of random states in which the next state depends on the present state only, not on the past. This is the Markov property. For a finite chain, the transition matrix P has entries p_ij = P(X_{n+1}=j | X_n=i), and each row sums to 1. The n-step probabilities are entries of P^n. A stationary distribution π satisfies πP = π and Σπ_i = 1.

Example: P = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]]. From π1 = 0.9π1 + 0.2π2, get 0.1π1 = 0.2π2, so π1 = 2π2. With π1 + π2 = 1, π = (2/3, 1/3). Check: (2/3)(0.9) + (1/3)(0.2) = 2/3.

sections.heading: Poisson and Brownian
sections.text:
A Poisson process N(t) counts events up to time t. It has independent and stationary increments, N(0)=0, and N(t) ~ Poisson(λt), so P(N(t)=k) = e^(−λt)(λt)^k/k!. Waiting times between events are independent exponential variables with mean 1/λ.

Brownian motion B(t) has continuous paths and independent, stationary Gaussian increments: B(0)=0 and B(t) − B(s) ~ N(0, t − s) for t > s. It is nowhere differentiable in the ordinary sense, so stochastic calculus is needed.

sections.heading: Martingales and stationarity
sections.text: A martingale is a process X_n with E|X_n| < ∞ and E(X_{n+1} | F_n) = X_n, where F_n is the information up to time n. It models a fair game: the expected next value equals the present value. A process is strictly stationary if every finite-dimensional distribution is unchanged by a time shift; it is weakly stationary if only mean and autocovariance are unchanged. Stationarity is a key assumption behind ergodic theorems, which link long-run time averages to expectations.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.text: In queueing, Markov chains describe the number in an M/M/1 system, where arrivals are Poisson, service times are exponential and there is a single server. In finance, geometric Brownian motion, where the log of the price follows a Brownian motion with drift, is a common model for asset prices; it is a martingale after discounting only when its drift equals the discount rate. In biology, branching processes model population growth and extinction, and Markov chains model gene or disease states. Check model assumptions against data.

keyPoints: Markov property: the next state depends only on the present state.
Stationary distribution of a finite Markov chain satisfies πP = π and Σπ_i = 1.
Poisson process: N(t) ~ Poisson(λt), and interarrival times are exponential with mean 1/λ.
Brownian motion has independent Gaussian increments with variance t − s.
A martingale satisfies E(X_{n+1} | F_n) = X_n.
Stationarity means distributions or moments are unchanged by time shifts; applications include queueing, finance and biology.

en.title: Research methods in mathematics
en.short: Literature search, choosing a problem, rigorous proof, writing, ethics and dissertation planning.

sections.heading: Finding the literature
sections.text: Start with a question, not papers. Search MathSciNet (subscription) and zbMATH Open (free) by keyword, author and review. arXiv holds preprints; they are not peer reviewed, so check whether a paper has since appeared in a journal. Use citation chaining: read a recent survey, then follow the references it cites and the papers that cite it. Keep a search log and a reference manager (Zotero or Mendeley) from day one. Access varies by institution; ask your library.

sections.heading: Choosing a problem
sections.text:
A good master’s problem is small, open and checkable. Look for a gap or an open question in a survey, then test feasibility: can you state it precisely, find examples, and finish within your time? Ask your supervisor to confirm it is open. Avoid a problem that needs machinery you do not have.

Case: Amina, a master’s student in Nigeria, reads a survey and finds an open question about a bound. She tests it on small examples, finds a counterexample, and with her supervisor narrows the question to a case she can settle. The counterexample becomes part of her result.

sections.heading: Proof, writing and talks
sections.text:
Rigour means every step follows from definitions, earlier results or stated hypotheses. Check edge cases (zero, empty set, equality) and look for a counterexample before you believe a claim. Exposition is part of the work: define terms, motivate the question, and separate the idea from the technical details.

Write in LaTeX, the standard in mathematics. Structure: abstract, introduction, results with proofs, references. A talk is not a paper: choose one idea, fit the time, and rehearse.

sections.heading: Ethics and planning
sections.text:
Research ethics covers plagiarism, fabrication and falsification, authorship, conflicts of interest and duplicate submission. Cite every source you use, including software and data. Rules on preprints, authorship order and simultaneous submission vary by journal and country; check official guidance.

Plan the dissertation backwards from the deadline: milestones for reading, first proof, a draft and a final version. Write early, keep backups, and meet your supervisor regularly.

keyPoints: Search MathSciNet and zbMATH Open, and treat arXiv preprints as unrefereed until published.
Choose a problem that is open, precisely stated and feasible within your course length.
A proof is rigorous only when every step is justified and edge cases are checked.
Write in LaTeX with a clear structure: abstract, introduction, results, proofs, references.
Cite all sources and follow your institution’s and the journal’s ethics rules; they vary.
Plan milestones backwards from the deadline and write from the start.
